diagrams.title: DC shunt motor model
diagrams.cap: Back EMF opposes the supply and limits I<sub>a</sub>; at start E<sub>b</sub> = 0, so a starter resistance is needed. Weakening the field (φ ↓) raises the speed.
diagrams.qq: V = 220 V, Ia = 20 A, Ra = 0.5 Ω. Back EMF?

diagrams.title: DC machine protection — what senses what
diagrams.cap: The NVC is wired in series with the shunt field, so if the field opens the starter releases at once — this protects against dangerous over-speed (N ∝ 1/φ).
diagrams.qq: Why is the NVC in series with the field? → Field loss → starter trips

diagrams.title: DC machine types by field connection
diagrams.cap: The field winding decides the type: separate supply, across the armature (shunt — many fine turns), in series with it (series — few thick turns), or both (compound). Current relations follow straight from the circuit.
diagrams.qq: Shunt generator: IL = 50 A, Ish = 2 A. Ia?

diagrams.title: DC generator vs DC motor
diagrams.cap: The same machine works both ways. As a generator the induced EMF exceeds the terminal voltage (E = V + I<sub>a</sub>R<sub>a</sub>); as a motor the back EMF is less than the supply (E<sub>b</sub> = V − I<sub>a</sub>R<sub>a</sub>).
diagrams.qq: Motor: V = 230 V, Ia = 10 A, Ra = 0.5 Ω. Eb?

diagrams.title: DC motor speed–torque characteristics
diagrams.cap: Shunt: almost constant speed. Series: speed falls steeply with load, very high at no load (never start unloaded). Compound: in between.
diagrams.qq: Which motor must never run on no load?

diagrams.title: DC generator OCC (magnetisation curve)
diagrams.cap: Voltage builds up to where the field-resistance line cuts the OCC. If R<sub>sh</sub> > R<sub>critical</sub> (the tangent), the generator fails to build up.

diagrams.title: DC generator external characteristics
diagrams.cap: Shunt voltage falls with load (I<sub>a</sub>R<sub>a</sub> drop + armature reaction + weaker field). Series voltage rises with load. Level/over-compound keeps it flat or rising.
diagrams.qq: Which generator's voltage rises with load?

why.cause: generator: speed ↑ or φ ↑ → E = PφZN/60A ↑

why.cause: differential compound: φ = φ<sub>sh</sub> − φ<sub>se</sub> → load ↑ → φ<sub>se</sub> ↑ → net φ ↓ → V falls steeply
why.effect: Nearly constant current → arc welding generators.

why.cause: series field short-circuited → φ<sub>se</sub> = 0 → differential: φ ↑ → E ↑ · cumulative: φ ↓ → E ↓
why.effect: E ∝ φN at constant speed (resistances ignored).

mistakes.m: "Every motor: more torque means less speed, T ∝ 1/N"
mistakes.c: Only the series motor behaves like that (T ∝ 1/N²). A shunt motor keeps nearly constant speed while torque changes. T ∝ 1/N also holds for a constant-power drive (P = Tω).

mistakes.m: "Differential compound: shorting the series field reduces the voltage"
mistakes.c: The series field was opposing the shunt field. Removing it raises the net flux, so the voltage rises: strictly 60 → 80 = +33.3 %; TNEB 2018 Q69 expects the option 'increases by 20 %'.

mistakes.m: Weakening the field slows a DC motor
mistakes.c: N ∝ E<sub>b</sub>/φ: a weaker field → higher speed.
